  the series color; labels, values, legends, and axis text use **text tokens**
  (primary / secondary / muted). A light categorical hue (yellow, aqua) is illegible
  as text on the surface. Identity comes from the colored mark *beside* the text - a
  dot, a short line-key, a swatch - never from coloring the text itself. A label set
  *inside* a colored fill (a stacked segment, a map tile) is the one exception: pick
  white or ink by the fill's luminance so it always clears contrast.
- **When end-labels collide, don't stack them.** Direct end-labels work when series
  separate at the right edge. When lines converge, nudging labels apart vertically
  detaches them from their lines and reads as noise - instead use **leader lines**
  (a thin connector from label to line-end), facet into **small multiples**, or fall
  back to the legend + tooltip. Past ~4 converging series, small multiples is usually right.

## Figures - when the form is a number

- **Stat tile** contract: `label` (sentence case, no trailing colon) · `value` (Sans
  semibold, auto-compact: 1,284 / 12.9K / $4.2M) · `delta` (optional; signed,
  vs a named period; color = direction × whether up is good) · `trend` (optional;
  12-point sparkline in the de-emphasis hue, current period in the accent).
- **Meter:** the fill carries severity (accent -> warning -> danger); the unfilled
  track is a **lighter step of the same ramp** (blue-on-blue, etc.) so state reads
  across the whole bar.
- **Hero figure.** The single number a dashboard leads with, >=48px, in the same
  sans as everything else (never a display or serif face - it reads as off-brand
  decoration). Exactly one per view.
- **Proportional figures for big numbers; tabular only in columns.** A large
  standalone value (hero figure, stat-tile value) uses the font's default
  proportional figures - `tabular-nums` gives every digit the width of a `0`, so a
  number like `121` looks loose at display sizes. Reserve
  `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` for columns of numbers that must align
  vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

## Texture - the backup channel (opt-in)

Where hue fails - full-severity CVD, grayscale print, `forced-colors` - texture
carries identity. One directional hand-drawn fill, used at **45° and its 135° mirror
only** (never horizontal/vertical - those read as gridlines/bars). Inked tone-on-tone
(a step from the fill's own ramp), equal loudness across slots. On value scales the
texture is *ordered* (rotation steps with magnitude; arm angle carries the diverging
sign) so it never misstates the value. Triggered by an accessibility setting, print,
or `forced-colors` - never on by default. (See `palette.md`.)
======
# Anti-patterns - what goes wrong

Check every chart against this list. If your output matches an entry, it is wrong -
fix it before shipping. These are real failure modes, each caught in shipping
dashboards.

## Color & encoding

**Bad: Dual-axis charts (two y-scales on one plot).**
Why it misleads: the alignment of the two scales is arbitrary, so the chart invents a
correlation that isn't in the data. Real example: an "Adoption" chart plotting Users
(0-30k) against Sessions (0-800k) - a reviewer flagged it as looking "hallucinated."
Good: Do instead: two charts, small multiples, or index both series to a common base
(=100 at t0) on **one** axis.

**Bad: Recolor-on-filter.** Assigning colors by current rank, so filtering out a series
repaints the survivors.
Why: a reader who learned "Acme is blue" is now misled.
Good: Color follows the entity, not its row number. Survivors keep their hue.

**Bad: Cycling / generating hues past 8.** A 9th categorical color, generated or reused.
Why: indistinguishable from an existing slot under CVD; breaks the order check.
Good: Fold the tail into "Other," facet into small multiples, or use composite encoding.

**Bad: Eyeballing colorblind-safety.** "These look different enough."
Good: Run `scripts/validate_palette.js`. Adjacent Delta E >= 8 (OKLab ×100), or 6-8 WITH secondary encoding.

**Bad: A value-ramp on nominal categories.** Coloring each bar darker-where-bigger
when the categories have no natural order (products, teams, endpoints).
Why: it double-encodes bar length as hue, burns the only free channel on
information the chart already shows, and fails the categorical checks by design
(a ramp spans the lightness band and drops below the chroma floor).
Good: One series -> one color (slot 1) for every bar. Ordered categories (funnel,
tiers, age bands) -> the ordinal ramp, validated with `--ordinal`.

**Bad: Rainbow / non-neighbor sequential.** A multi-hue ramp for magnitude.
Good: One hue, light->dark. (Analogous neighbors or semantic heat are the only multi-hue
sequential exceptions, always with a scale legend.)

**Bad: A hue at the diverging midpoint, or two cool hues as the two poles.**
Why: the midpoint must read as "nothing"; poles must read as opposite. blue<->aqua
fails this (both cool); blue<->red or blue<->orange succeed (warm/cool).
Good: Two hues that read as opposite + a neutral gray midpoint.

**Bad: Status color used for a non-status series** (or a series color used for status).
Good: Status tokens only when the color *means* good/bad; categorical when it's identity.

## Form

**Bad: Eight categorical hues when the story is one number.** The most common way a
chart misses its point.
Good: Emphasis (highlight one, gray the rest), or a stat tile / hero number.

**Bad: A one-bar bar chart, or a 2-slice pie.**
Good: A stat tile. The number is the chart.

**Bad: A donut/pie for comparing close values.**
Good: A bar, or the numbers. Part-to-whole at a glance only, <= 6 segments.

**Bad: More than ~7 color classes carrying meaning.**
Good: A table, or table + chart. Past ~7 bins, adjacent classes blur.

## Marks & chrome

**Bad: Thick saturated blocks, heavy gridlines, no breathing room.** Reads loud, even
childish, at scale.
Good: Thin marks, hairline recessive grid/axes, generous padding. Saturated fills are
for small marks and accents, never large blocks.

**Bad: Dashed gridlines or axis rules.** Dashing adds visual noise and reads as
"projection" or "threshold" when it's just a grid.
Good: Gridlines and axes are solid hairlines, one shade off the surface.

**Bad: A number on every data point.** A value beside every dot or segment is chaos and goes unread.
Good: A legend is always present for >= 2 series; direct-label *selectively* (the endpoint, the extreme, the one series that matters) and let the axis + tooltip carry the rest.

**Bad: A border drawn around marks to separate them.**
Good: A 2px surface gap between fills (stacked segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring (on overlapping markers).

**Bad: A label clipped by, or overflowing, a too-small bar or stacked segment** -
including `overflow: hidden` cropping the first/last characters of an in-segment label.
Good: Only render a label inside a mark when it fits with padding; otherwise move it
outside the bar end, or drop it to the tooltip/legend (the value stays in the table view).

**Bad: A chart container whose fixed height excludes the x-axis band** - the plot
fits, the axis labels don't, so the card gets a tiny nested vertical scroll.
Good: Size the container to include the axis labels (plot height + x-axis band),
or let the container grow with its content instead of fixing a height.

**Bad: A display or serif face on the hero figure.** It reads as off-brand decoration.
Good: The hero figure uses the same sans as everything else.

**Bad: `tabular-nums` on a large standalone number.** Equal-width digits make `121`
look loose at display sizes.
Good: Proportional figures on hero and stat-tile values; `tabular-nums` only where
numbers align vertically (table rows, axis ticks).

**Bad: Texture on by default, or as decoration.** Dense angled fields are a vestibular
risk and read as noise on value scales.
Good: Texture is opt-in (a11y setting, print, forced-colors), 45°/135° only, ordered on
value scales.

## Interaction & accessibility

**Bad: A tooltip as the only way to read a value.**
Good: Tooltips enhance, never gate - every value is also reachable via direct labels or
the table view; keyboard focus shows the same as hover.

**Bad: Pinpoint hover targets - an 8px scatter dot you must land on dead-center.**
Good: The hit area includes the 2px gap and meets a ~24px minimum; dense scatter uses a nearest-point / Voronoi layer.

**Bad: Per-chart filters, or filters inside a chart card.**
Good: One filter row above everything it scopes; all charts re-render against the same slice.

**Bad: Skeleton flash on refetch.**
Good: Hold the previous render at reduced opacity - no layout jump.

**Bad: No table view / color-only encoding on a continuous scale.**
Good: Every chart has a table-view twin (the WCAG-clean equivalent).

"""Two normal curves for a standardised mean difference of 0.72 (imagery training vs no exercise).

Pooled effect and interval as recorded in the project's pilot evidence map (docs/research-project.md,
"Strength from imagined contractions": Paravlic et al. 2018, 13 studies, 370 participants, ES 0.72 [0.42, 1.02]).
Derived figures assume normal distributions with equal SDs and are computed below, not typed.
"""
import math
import sys

import matplotlib
matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import font_manager

OUT = sys.argv[1]
D, LO, HI = 0.72, 0.42, 1.02
K_STUDIES, N_PEOPLE = 13, 370

phi = lambda x: 0.5 * (1 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2)))
pdf = lambda x, m: math.exp(-0.5 * (x - m) ** 2) / math.sqrt(2 * math.pi)
u3, u3_lo, u3_hi = phi(D), phi(LO), phi(HI)          # share of the trained group above the control mean
ps = phi(D / math.sqrt(2))                            # chance a random trained person beats a random control
ovl = 2 * phi(-D / 2)                                 # overlap of the two curves
pct = lambda v: f"{round(v * 100)}%"

SURFACE, INK, INK2, MUTED, AXIS = "#fcfcfb", "#0b0b0b", "#52514e", "#898781", "#c3c2b7"
BLUE = "#2a78d6"

for f in ("LiberationSans-Regular.ttf", "LiberationSans-Bold.ttf"):
    font_manager.fontManager.addfont("/usr/share/fonts/truetype/liberation/" + f)
plt.rcParams.update({"font.family": "Liberation Sans", "font.size": 10.5, "text.color": INK})

xs = [-3.4 + i * 0.01 for i in range(781)]
ctrl = [pdf(x, 0) for x in xs]
img = [pdf(x, D) for x in xs]
peak = pdf(0, 0)

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(8, 4.9), dpi=200, facecolor=SURFACE)
ax = fig.add_axes([0.06, 0.25, 0.9, 0.52], facecolor=SURFACE)

ax.fill_between(xs, ctrl, color=MUTED, alpha=0.10, linewidth=0)
ax.fill_between(xs, img, color=BLUE, alpha=0.10, linewidth=0)
ax.plot(xs, ctrl, color=MUTED, linewidth=2, solid_capstyle="round")
ax.plot(xs, img, color=BLUE, linewidth=2, solid_capstyle="round")

# Means: thin solid rules from the baseline to each peak.
ax.plot([0, 0], [0, peak], color=MUTED, linewidth=1)
ax.plot([D, D], [0, peak], color=BLUE, linewidth=1)

# The shift and its 95% interval, drawn above the peaks.
yw = peak * 1.12
ax.plot([LO, HI], [yw, yw], color=BLUE, linewidth=1.6, solid_capstyle="round")
for xv in (LO, HI):
    ax.plot([xv, xv], [yw - peak * 0.03, yw + peak * 0.03], color=BLUE, linewidth=1.6)
ax.plot([D], [yw], marker="o", markersize=6.5, color=BLUE, markeredgecolor=SURFACE, markeredgewidth=1.6)
ax.text(HI + 0.08, yw, f"Shift {D:.2f} SD  (95% CI {LO:.2f} to {HI:.2f})", va="center", ha="left",
        fontsize=10, color=INK)

# Direct labels: ink text, identity from the coloured key beside it.
def key_label(x, y, color, text, ha):
    ax.plot([x - 0.32, x - 0.06] if ha == "left" else [x + 0.06, x + 0.32], [y, y], color=color, linewidth=2.5,
            solid_capstyle="round")
    ax.text(x if ha == "left" else x, y, text, va="center", ha="left" if ha == "left" else "right", fontsize=10,
            color=INK)

key_label(-3.0, pdf(-1.25, 0) + 0.035, MUTED, "", "left")
ax.text(-2.66, pdf(-1.25, 0) + 0.035, "No-exercise controls", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=10, color=INK)
ax.plot([2.25, 2.51], [pdf(2.0, D) + 0.035] * 2, color=BLUE, linewidth=2.5, solid_capstyle="round")
ax.text(2.59, pdf(2.0, D) + 0.035, "Imagery training", va="center", ha="left", fontsize=10, color=INK)

# Axes: one hairline baseline, integer ticks in SD units, no y scale (density has no reader meaning here).
ax.set_xlim(-3.4, 4.4)
ax.set_ylim(0, peak * 1.25)
for side in ("left", "right", "top"):
    ax.spines[side].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(AXIS)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_linewidth(0.8)
ax.set_yticks([])
ax.set_xticks(range(-3, 5))
ax.set_xticklabels([("+" if t > 0 else "") + str(t) if t != 0 else "0" for t in range(-3, 5)], color=INK2)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", colors=AXIS, labelcolor=INK2, length=3, width=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Strength, in standard deviations from the control-group average", color=INK2, fontsize=10,
              labelpad=6)

fig.text(0.06, 0.93, f"Imagined contractions shift strength by {D:.2f} standard deviations", fontsize=15,
         fontweight="bold", color=INK, ha="left")
fig.text(0.06, 0.875, f"The average trained person outscores about {pct(u3)} of untrained controls "
         f"(pooled across {K_STUDIES} studies, {N_PEOPLE} participants)", fontsize=10.5, color=INK2, ha="left")

fig.text(0.06, 0.105,
         f"If both groups are normally distributed with equal spread: {pct(u3)} of the trained group sits above the control "
         f"average ({pct(u3_lo)} to {pct(u3_hi)} across the 95% CI);\n"
         f"a random trained person beats a random control {pct(ps)} of the time; the two curves overlap by {pct(ovl)}.",
         fontsize=8.6, color=INK2, ha="left", linespacing=1.45)
fig.text(0.06, 0.035,
         "Source: Paravlic et al. 2018, Sports Med 48:1165–1187, as recorded in the project’s pilot evidence map "
         "(not yet re-extracted by the review).", fontsize=8, color=MUTED, ha="left")

fig.savefig(OUT, facecolor=SURFACE)
print(f"U3 {u3:.4f} [{u3_lo:.4f}, {u3_hi:.4f}]  PS {ps:.4f}  OVL {ovl:.4f}")

The chart is above. The grey curve is the no-exercise controls, centred on 0. The blue curve is the imagery-trained group, shifted 0.72 standard deviations to the right. The bar above the peaks is the 95% confidence interval for that shift, 0.42 to 1.02.

What the shift means, if both groups are bell-shaped with the same spread:
- **76%** of the trained group sits above the control average (66% to 85% across the confidence interval).
- **69%** is the chance that a random trained person beats a random control.
- **72%** of the two curves overlap, so most trained and untrained people still fall in the same range.

All three percentages depend on two assumptions:
- Both groups are bell-shaped with equal spread.
- The 0.72 is measured in units of how much strength varies between people. The research document records it only as "ES 0.72". If Paravlic standardised the strength gains some other way, for example against the variation in people's change scores, these percentages would change. That gets settled when the review extracts the paper.

The chart isn't saved to the repository or any document; it was sent only to you.

content.text:
You're right about the test bench, and I take back calling it a weak choice. An effect that's already established (13 studies pooled, High certainty) is exactly what you'd use as a positive control, because a sound method should get it back. The review's dry run already works this way, and a positive-control arm in the primary study is a design choice for Gate 8.

Your other three claims don't hold:

- **A test bench can't carry results over to other questions.** It shows the method works; it says nothing about meditation, focus or visualisation in general, or about health. Each of those needs its own outcome data. The project's sources keep showing the gap: neurofeedback control is rated High certainty, yet its clinical effect with blinded raters was a standardised difference of 0.04 across 20 trials. In the real-time fMRI trial, pain fell as much with sham feedback as with real feedback. The research document says it plainly: "the brain-signal control is well established, the clinical benefits attached to it mostly are not." It also deliberately leaves clinical benefit out of its ratings.
- **Correlations can't demonstrate benefit.** The 0.72 comes from comparisons of trained groups against controls, which is stronger evidence than correlation. Moving to correlations would weaken the case, not prove it.
- **"Slower muscle atrophy" isn't what was shown.** Clark 2014, as the research document records it, reports strength loss, not muscle size. Its title points to the brain as the source of the effect, so what it shows is slower loss of strength. On "when working out": the sources compare imagery with doing no exercise, and physical training beat imagery by 0.42 where the two were compared directly. None of them tests imagery added to a workout. The closest evidence is attention during lifting (Schoenfeld 2018: one trial, 30 untrained men, larger growth in the biceps but none in the quadriceps), rated Moderate.

Nobody disputes that strength is good for health. What hasn't been shown is that the mental route leads to health outcomes. Adding health outcomes to the review would change its scope, and that would be settled in the Gate 2 protocol.

content.text:
In the simplest terms: **imagining hard contractions of a muscle, without moving it, makes that muscle stronger than doing nothing, though real training makes it stronger still.**

- Across 13 studies (370 people): strength rose 0.72 standard deviations against no exercise, and 1.05 with real training. Where the two were compared directly, real training beat imagery by 0.42.
- One 12-week trial: little-finger strength rose 35% and elbow strength 13.5%, with 8 people per group.
- With the hand immobilised for 4 weeks, imagery roughly halved the strength lost: 24% against 45%.

A separate gate for this makes sense, and it fixes a real gap. The Gate 1 dry run uses one study per ability, so it never tests pooling on real data (R-028). This would. The shape I'd propose:

- **G1b, positive-control reproduction.** It opens after Gate 1, runs alongside Stage 2, and must be Approved before Stage 3 (search and screening) starts.
- **Deliverable:** the full pipeline run on the primary studies that Paravlic 2018 pooled for imagery against no exercise. That means two blinded extractors, reconciliation, effect sizes, both pooling methods, a GRADE draft and a reviewer audit.
- **Acceptance:**
  - The pooled estimate lands inside 0.42 to 1.02, or every difference is traced to a choice of study or formula.
  - Every number carries provenance.
  - The reviewer's report has no open failure.
- **Conditions:**
  - You get Paravlic's list of included studies and their full texts.
  - The result validates the method only and never enters the review's results (the same rule as the pilot), and the protocol says it was done.
  - The two parallel extractors need their own approval line at this gate, because charter decision 7 defers multi-agent workflows to Gates 3 and 4.

Shall I add G1b to the Stage gates table in the live plan, marked Not submitted, with that deliverable and acceptance?

from.content: Ten gates separate charter, team setup, a positive-control reproduction, protocol and pre-registration, search and screening, extraction and risk of bias, the statistical analysis plan, results, manuscript submission and the go/no-go decision on the primary study.

target.text: the one-week overlaps are the only slack in the 18 weeks.

from.content: the one-week overlaps are the only slack in the 18 weeks. Stage 1b, the positive-control reproduction, runs alongside Stage 2 in weeks 3 and 4, and Stage 3 starts only when both G1b and G2 are approved.

**Stage 1b, positive-control reproduction (weeks 3 to 4, alongside Stage 2).** The head agent runs the full pipeline on the primary studies that Paravlic et al. 2018 pooled for motor imagery versus no exercise: two blinded extraction agents, reconciliation, effect sizes, frequentist and Bayesian pooling, a GRADE draft and the reviewer's audit. The pipeline must recover the published pooled estimate (0.72, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.02) or explain every difference. Sean stages the included-study list and full texts and approves the parallel extractors as a line item at G1b. The results validate the method only and never enter the review's results. Hand-over: reproduction report with the pooled estimate against the target, discrepancy log, reviewer report.
